October 1948
Treasury Financing Operations
September-October Certificate and Note Maturities

On August 9, the Secretary of the Treasury announced as a further anti-inflationary move the raising of the rates on new short-term Government securities. The Secretary stated his intention to offer a one-year 1-1/4 percent certificate in exchange for the two issues of 1 percent certificates and the 1 percent Treasury notes maturing October 1, and to offer a 1-3/8 percent Treasury note maturing April 1, 1950, in exchange for the four and one-half year 1-1/2 percent Treasury notes maturing on September 15. It was stated also that the rate of interest on Treasury savings notes would be adjusted and made effective on the new issue available September 1.

The announcement stated further that the 2-1/2 percent partially tax-exempt Treasury bonds maturing in the amount of $451 million on September 15, 1948, would be paid off in cash. The Secretary said also that there would be no change in the Government's policy with regard to the long-term Treasury bonds.

Subsription books for the 1-3/8 per cent Treasury notes were opened September 1 and were closed at the close of business on September 3. Subscriptions were invited at par, in exchange for the 1-1/2 per cent Treasury notes maturing September 15, 1948. The new notes were dated September 15, 1948, and bear interest from that date at the rate of 1-3/8 per cent per annum, payable on a semi-annual basis on April 1 and October 1, 1949, and April 1, 1950. They will mature April 1, 1950, and will not be subject to call for redemption prior to maturity. The notes were issued in bearer form only in denominations of $1,000, $5,000, $10,000, $100,000, and $1,000,000.

Reports to the Treasury on the ownership of Government securities indicate that on July 30, 1948, about 73 percent of the $3,748 million of the 1-1/2 percent notes maturing September 15 were owned by Federal Reserve Banks and reporting commercial banks, and about 75 percent of the $451 million of the 2-1/2 percent bonds maturing September 15 were owned by reporting commercial banks. The ownership figures for July 30 are the latest which are available for holdings of commercial banks. Subscriptions for the new 1-3/8 percent notes totaled $3,596 million, leaving $152 million to be paid in cash.
Call of 2 Percent Treasury Bonds of 1948-50

On August 13, the Secretary announced that all outstanding 2 percent Treasury bonds of 1948-50, dated December 8, 1939, are called for redemption on December 15, 1948. The announcement stated that holders of these bonds may, in advance of the redemption date, be offered the privilege of exchanging all or part of their called bonds for other interest-bearing obligations of the United States, in which event public notice will hereafter be given.
Treasury Savings Notes, Series D

Details of the new Treasury savings notes, Series D, which became available for purchase on September 1, 1946, and the ending of the sale of Treasury savings notes, Series C, at the close of business August 31, were announced by the Treasury on August 18.

The new notes of Series D will be dated as of the first day of the month in which purchased. will mature three years thereafter, and will be issued at par. Interest on the notas will accrue each month from month of issue, on a graduated scale, the equivalent yield if held to maturity being approximately 1.40 percent per annum. Information relating to capital movements between the United States and foreign countries is presented in four sections. Section IV contains data for recent months on outstanding contracts of banks for forward purchases and sales of foreign exchange.

The data in these four sections are based on reports filed each month by banks, bankers, and brokers throughout the United States. The reports are collected, checked, and tabulated by the twelve Federal Reserve Banks. The totals are then forwarded to the Treasury Department for consolidation and publication.
